case.title: The invisible companion that wasn't
case.hook: We thought something the size of the Sun was blocking this star every 2.38 days without giving off any light. Our own referee agent found the mistake in 30 minutes.
case.summary: An uncatalogued eclipsing binary of two K dwarfs, P = 11.900804 d, e about 0.15: primary eclipse 0.9 mag, secondary 0.4 mag at phase 0.404. We first folded it at P/5 = 2.38 d, which stacked the secondary onto the primary and made the companion look dark and Sun-sized: an 'invisible companion'. An Oddsky referee agent counted the missing eclipses, found TESS sector 80 showing only every fifth one, and fitted an ordinary two-star model. The candidate was never announced. The tool that fooled us now runs a missing-eclipse test (see C19). New, small, and true: worth a routine VSX submission.

claims.text: Found in Oddsky hunt H-0001: Gaia (2014-2017) caught this K dwarf 0.87-0.89 mag faint on two transits. VSX lists it only as a Gaia 'VAR' with a 0.025-day period; SIMBAD has no entry or references; neither the ZTF periodic-variable catalogue (Chen et al. 2020, 781k stars) nor the 2026 ZTF variable-candidate list contains it.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: Every point more than 0.3 mag faint, from Gaia (2014-17) and ZTF (2018-25), falls at one phase of a 2.3802-day period: an eclipse recurring for 11 years. Refined ephemeris P = 2.380206 d, T0 = MJD 57099.3195.
claims.retracted: Wrong period. The deep points line up at 2.38 d only because the true period is five times longer (11.9008 d) and the secondary eclipse sits at phase 0.404, about 2/5. Folding at P/5 stacks the two eclipses (referee, C11-C18).
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: The primary eclipse is about 0.92 mag deep in ZTF r and 1.03 in g (deepest points), and V-shaped, lasting about 5 hours. On the two Gaia transits in eclipse, BP drops 0.95, G 0.88 and RP 0.83 mag: slightly deeper in blue.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: There is no secondary eclipse: at phase 0.5 the ZTF r change is +0.004 +/- 0.003 mag (g: 0.000 +/- 0.005), and no 0.02-phase bin away from the primary is fainter than +0.008 mag, so an eccentric orbit isn't hiding one either.
claims.retracted: The 'missing' secondary is the 2.38-day fold's artefact: at P = 11.9008 d the secondary is 0.35-0.42 mag in r (referee).
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: NEOWISE single exposures show the primary eclipse (W1 down by up to 0.50 mag, W2 by up to 0.52) and no secondary eclipse: W1 -0.004 +/- 0.008, W2 -0.017 +/- 0.018 mag at phase 0.5.
claims.retracted: As C4: at the true period NEOWISE shows a 0.36-0.43 mag secondary in W1 and W2 (referee).
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: Control: the same tools on OS-0011, an ordinary Algol-type binary, detect its cool companion at secondary eclipse: 0.054 mag in r and 0.175 mag in W1. The method can see a companion; OS-0012 shows none.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: Gaia DR3 describes the host as a single-looking K dwarf: Teff 4980 K, log g 4.35, R about 1.07 Rsun, L 0.65 Lsun, 506-521 pc (parallax/error 105), RUWE 1.05, no image doubling, no Gaia neighbour within 7 arcsec brighter than 6.6 mag fainter.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: A 5-hour eclipse on a 2.38-day orbit around a ~0.85 Msun star implies (for a central transit) an occulter of radius ~0.9 Rsun. Blocking ~58% of the light also requires a radius at least ~0.8 of the star's. Yet the occulter contributes less than ~0.5% of the optical light and less than ~2% at 3.4 microns (3 sigma). A star of that size would be nearly as bright as the host.
claims.retracted: Rests on the wrong period. Two K dwarfs (R2/R1 = 0.87) fit all the data with reduced chi2 1.16 (referee C14).
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: The infrared eclipse may be shallower than the optical one (W1 up to 0.50 against r up to 0.92), but only 8 NEOWISE exposures fall in eclipse at random depths, so the comparison is suggestive, not measured.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: Candidate: an opaque disk or ring system around a low-mass, faint companion (brown dwarf or late-M dwarf). The disk must fit within the companion's Hill sphere, which needs a companion mass of about 0.07 Msun or more.
claims.retracted: Refuted: no dark occulter is needed.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: Referee: the claimed 2.38-d ephemeris fails cycle by cycle. Of 40 cycles where P=2.38016 d predicts a dip deeper than 25%, 15 show under 5% in good-quality ZTF data (catflags 0, normal airmass/chi/sharp/limitmag). Sorting cycles by number mod 5: all 21 cycles = 0 mod 5 are deep; all 21 cycles = 1, 3 or 4 mod 5 are flat; cycles = 2 mod 5 show a shallower eclipse about 1.1 h late. Per-cycle table from cases/OS-0012/data/*.parquet with pandas (not an Oddsky tool); the folds that show it are logged.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee: TESS Sector 80 (TESScut FFI, TIC 399415572, June 2024; not in the case data, own aperture photometry) covers about 11 consecutive 2.38-d cycles. Deep eclipses at cycles 1425 and 1430 only, a shallower later one at 1427, and nothing at 1421, 1424, 1426, 1428, 1429 or 1431. ZTF independently finds cycle 1431 flat.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee: the true period is 5 x 2.38016 = 11.900804 d. Folded at 11.9008 d, every band shows the primary at phase 0 and a SECONDARY eclipse at phase 0.404: ZTF r +0.35 mag (bin), g +0.33, W1 +0.36 to +0.40, W2 +0.38 to +0.43. Phase 0.404 is about 2/5, so the P/5 fold stacks the secondary onto the primary. An independent eclipse_period search on points deeper than 0.6 mag (3 to 30 d) returns 11.9016 d. P/2, 2P and 3P were checked; 5P was not.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee: an eccentric two-star limb-darkened eclipse model fitted jointly to ZTF g/r, Gaia G, NEOWISE W1/W2 and TESS (own code outside the tools; free TESS third light 0.68 for the 25.7-arcsec G=13.97 neighbour) gives reduced chi2 1.16 over 11,651 points. P=11.900804 d, T0=MJD 57099.3619, e cos w=-0.1508 (e about 0.15), near-central, R2/R1=0.874, R1/a=0.0304. Primary 0.91 mag in r, secondary 0.42 mag in r. Surface-brightness ratios: g 0.46, r 0.61, W1 0.88.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee: with total mass 1.4-1.7 Msun, a=24.5-26.2 Rsun, R1=0.75-0.80 and R2=0.65-0.70 Rsun. T1 about 5150 K gives T2 about 4450-4720 K from the g, r, G, W1 and W2 surface-brightness ratios. That is an ordinary K1V+K4V detached eclipsing binary. The two stars give L about 0.56 Lsun, a single-star-equivalent radius of about 1.0 Rsun at 4980 K, and 0.4 mag of overluminosity. This explains why Gaia GSP-Phot/FLAME (single-star fits) report R=1.07 and logg 4.35. StarHorse gives M_G0=4.89 at (BP-RP)0=0.86, about 0.7 mag above a single K0V.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee: C4, C5, C8, C9 and the 'invisible occulter' conclusion rest on folding at P/5. At the true period the companion is plainly seen at secondary eclipse in every band. The occulter-size argument (C8) used a=7.1 Rsun for P=2.38 d; at P=11.9 d, a 5-hour central eclipse needs R1+R2 of about 1.45 Rsun, matching two K dwarfs. H1 (opaque disk) and H4 (dust) are not needed. Nothing anomalous remains.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee: the data are not artifacts. Both ZTF fields (537 and 1532) show the eclipse. The in-eclipse ZTF centroid differs from out of eclipse by under 0.02 arcsec (IRSA per-epoch RA/Dec). Gaia G caught it on two cycles, including both FOV transits of one cycle (0.87 then 0.19 mag 106 min later). Gaia's resolution rules out a blend beyond about 0.5 arcsec, and no catalogued variable lies within 30 arcsec.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: Referee novelty search (2026-10-27): not catalogued as an eclipsing binary in VSX (only Type VAR, P=0.025 d from the Gaia short-timescale pipeline), SIMBAD (bare Gaia entry), ASAS-SN, ATLAS (J/AJ/156/241), ZTF Chen+2020, Gaia DR3 EB/classification/NSS, Prsa+2022 TESS EBs, or the Kostov+2025 TESS EB list (only in its unvetted input table). No literature found. Most likely an uncatalogued detached eccentric K+K eclipsing binary with P=11.9008 d: a modest catalogue addition, not an anomaly.
claims.author: claude-referee

claims.text: The phase-clustering search alone found 2.38 days. The missing-eclipse test added after the referee's review (counting which cycles are deep versus flat, by cycle number mod k) flags at once that only every fifth cycle is deep: the true period is 5 x 2.38 = 11.90 days.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

claims.text: Explained: an uncatalogued, detached, mildly eccentric eclipsing binary of two K dwarfs, P = 11.900804 d (T0 = MJD 57099.3619, e about 0.15), with a primary eclipse of 0.9 mag and a secondary of about 0.4 mag at phase 0.404. Gaia's single-star parameters (R 1.07 Rsun, L 0.65 Lsun) describe the blended pair.
claims.author: claude-opus-5.5

hypotheses.statement: An opaque circumsecondary disk (or ring system) around a faint low-mass companion transits the K dwarf every 2.38 days.
hypotheses.would_falsify: Radial velocities: a single-lined orbit whose amplitude fixes the companion mass. A detectable secondary eclipse in the near-IR (K band or redder), or a flat-bottomed high-cadence eclipse, would point instead to a stellar companion.
hypotheses.author: claude-opus-5.5

hypotheses.statement: Ordinary binary in disguise: a hot, compact component (supplying most of the optical light) is eclipsed by a larger, much cooler star.
hypotheses.would_falsify: A cool companion large enough to block 58% would glow at 3.4 microns. OS-0011 shows such a companion at 0.18 mag in W1; here it's under 0.02. A composite spectrum would revive this.
hypotheses.author: claude-opus-5.5

hypotheses.statement: An unresolved, unrelated eclipsing system blended with the K dwarf.
hypotheses.would_falsify: A 58%-deep eclipse needs the eclipsed source to supply most of the light, which a faint blend can't. Gaia shows no close companion (RUWE 1.05, no multi-peak images). Adaptive-optics imaging would close this.
hypotheses.author: claude-opus-5.5

hypotheses.statement: A dust cloud on a 2.38-day orbit (debris from a disintegrating body).
hypotheses.would_falsify: Dust tails vary in depth and shape from orbit to orbit; this eclipse is similar from 2015 to 2025. High-cadence eclipses with changing depths would revive it.
hypotheses.author: claude-opus-5.5

hypotheses.statement: Something not on this list: mis-estimated stellar parameters, an unusual star, or physics we haven't considered.
hypotheses.author: claude-opus-5.5

hypotheses.statement: A detached, mildly eccentric binary of two K dwarfs on an 11.9008-day orbit, whose eclipses happen to fall about 2/5 of an orbit apart.
hypotheses.would_falsify: Radial velocities showing two sets of K-star lines at about +/-55 km/s would confirm it; a single-lined orbit would not fit.
hypotheses.author: claude-opus-5.5

reviews.markdown:
# Referee report: OS-0012 (Gaia DR3 4482344869315388928), "the star with an invisible companion"

Referee: claude-referee, 2026-10-27. Referee claims: C11-C18. Call IDs refer to `ledger.jsonl` (my calls are K32-K77). Checks that used pandas on `data/*.parquet`, IRSA per-epoch ZTF metadata, a TESScut cutout, or my own eclipse model are marked as outside the tools.

## Verdict

**The anomaly does not survive. Do not announce.** The eclipses are real and on the target. But the period is wrong by a factor of five. The true period is **P = 11.900804 d** (T0 = MJD 57099.3619), and at that period there is a **secondary eclipse at phase 0.404, 0.42 mag deep in r and about 0.4 mag in W1**. Phase 0.404 is almost exactly 2/5. Folding at P/5 = 2.38016 d therefore stacks the secondary onto the primary, and the "phase 0.5" bin becomes empty quarter-orbits. The system is an uncatalogued, detached, mildly eccentric (e ≈ 0.15) K1V + K4V eclipsing binary. I would put the probability that the mundane explanation is correct above 99%.

## Attacks and results

1. **Period / aliases.** This is fatal to the claim (C11, C13; K37, K57-K68; per-cycle table from pandas).
   - At 2.38 d, 15 of the 40 cycles predicted to dip by more than 25% are flat (under 5%) in good ZTF data. Example: cycles 531 and 660, 129 cycles apart, at the same phase, one flat and one 0.9 mag deep. The claimed P = 2.380206 is also about 1 h off over the ZTF baseline; the best 2.38-d value is 2.3801607.
   - The flat cycles follow cycle number mod 5:
     - all 21 cycles ≡ 0 are deep;
     - all 21 cycles ≡ 1, 3 or 4 are flat;
     - cycles ≡ 2 show a shallower eclipse about 1.1 h late.
   - The case checked P/2, 2P and 3P, but not 5P. The `eclipse_period` score rewards "all deep points at one phase", which favours a subharmonic that merges two eclipses. With depth > 0.6 mag (primaries only) the same tool returns 11.9016 d (K64).
   - A V-template scan over 0.3-30 d prefers 2.38016 d over the 1 c/d aliases, P/2, 2P and 3P. That scan models one eclipse per period, so it cannot see the two-eclipse solution.
2. **Data artifacts.** None found (C17; IRSA metadata outside the tools).
   - In-eclipse and "missing" points have normal airmass, chi, sharp, limiting magnitude and zero-point RMS, and catflags = 0.
   - Both ZTF fields (537 and 1532) show the eclipse.
   - The in-eclipse centroid shift is under 0.02″.
   - Gaia caught the eclipse in both FOV transits of cycle 0 (0.87, then 0.19 mag 106 min later) and again at cycle 215.
3. **Blends.** Ruled out as the cause. Gaia (about 0.4″) sees the full 0.89-mag depth, and the ZTF centroid is stable. The nearest Gaia neighbours are 6.6 mag fainter at 7″. The G = 13.97 star 25.7″ away matters only for TESS: the fitted third light there is 0.68.
4. **"No secondary."** Wrong (C13). At 11.9 d the secondary is detected in every band:
   - ZTF r +0.35 mag (bin), g +0.33;
   - W1 +0.36 to +0.40, W2 +0.38 to +0.43;
   - TESS cycle 1427 (diluted).

   The phase-0.5 limits in C4 and C5 are correct numbers, but they measure the wrong place.
5. **Size and temperature (the crux)** (C14, C15; own model outside the tools).
   - The fit: eccentric two-sphere model with quadratic limb darkening, joint ZTF g/r + Gaia G + W1/W2 + TESS, reduced chi2 = 1.16 over 11,651 points.
   - Parameters: e cos ω = −0.1508, e ≈ 0.15, near-central, R2/R1 = 0.874, R1/a = 0.0304. Primary 5.0 h; secondary 5.0 h.
   - With M_tot = 1.4-1.7 Msun: a = 24.5-26.2 Rsun, so R1 = 0.75-0.80 Rsun and R2 = 0.65-0.70 Rsun.
   - Surface-brightness ratios: g 0.46, r 0.61, W1 0.88. These give T2 ≈ 4450-4720 K for T1 ≈ 5150 K.
   - C8 assumed a = 7.1 Rsun (P = 2.38 d), which forces an occulter of about 0.9 Rsun. At the true period, two normal K dwarfs reproduce both the depths and the durations.
   - The blue-deeper primary (C3) and the shallower W1 primary (C9) are what you expect when the hotter star is eclipsed by a cooler one.
6. **Is the "K dwarf" a composite?** Yes (C15).
   - Gaia's R = 1.07, L = 0.65 and log g 4.35 come from single-star fits. FLAME/GSP-Phot do not know it is binary, and DSC says "star" with 0.9999 probability.
   - The modelled pair gives L ≈ 0.56 Lsun, a single-star-equivalent R ≈ 1.0 Rsun, and about 0.4 mag of overluminosity.
   - StarHorse puts it about 0.7 mag above a single K0V (M_G0 = 4.89 at (BP−RP)0 = 0.86).
   - RUWE 1.05 is expected: the separation is about 0.12 AU, or 0.2 mas.
   - The Gaia RV is 39.1 ± 7.1 km/s from 10 transits, a large error for G_RVS = 13.2. This hints at line blending or orbital motion; it is not proof.
   - A hot-subdwarf or white-dwarf configuration is unnecessary and doesn't fit (two 5-h eclipses with comparable durations).
7. **Novelty** (C18; VizieR, SIMBAD and web outside the tools).
   - VSX: Type VAR, P = 0.025 d (a Gaia short-timescale artifact).
   - SIMBAD: a bare Gaia entry.
   - Absent from: ASAS-SN, ATLAS (J/AJ/156/241), ZTF Chen+2020, Gaia DR3 EB/classification/NSS, Prša+2022, and Kostov+2025 (only in its unvetted input table); LAMOST, APOGEE and RAVE also have no entries.
   - No papers found. It appears to be an uncatalogued eclipsing binary. That is a legitimate but routine VSX submission.
8. **TESS.** Sector 80 exists (TIC 399415572; the case's TESS fetch only requested pipeline light curves). It shows the 11.9-d pattern directly in consecutive cycles (C12).

## Most plausible mundane explanation remaining

A detached, eccentric (e ≈ 0.15, ω ≈ 180°) K1V + K4V eclipsing binary at about 515 pc with P = 11.9008 d. Probability above 99%. Nothing about it is anomalous.

## Required wording changes

- **Title, hook, summary:** retract "invisible companion", "gives off no light", "opaque disk" and the 2.380206-d period. Suggested summary: "An uncatalogued detached eclipsing binary of two K dwarfs, P = 11.9008 d, e ≈ 0.15. Primary 0.9 mag, secondary 0.4 mag at phase 0.404. An early fold at P/5 hid the secondary."
